Government Risk Register Warns: A National Power Cut Would Hit Britain “Instantaneously and Without Warning” — And Fewer Than 1 in 4 Britons Have the One Thing the Government Tells Every Home to Keep

Published 16 November 2026 · Helora — UK Readiness Report

The UK government’s own National Risk Register lists a national power outage among the risks it rates “Catastrophic”. Its words: All consumers without backup generators would lose their mains electricity supply instantaneously and without warning.

Not the blackout itself. What comes after it.

The moment the grid drops, you lose everything at once — the lights, the boiler, the news, and any way to call for help. And every backup you own to get through it — the torch batteries, the phone, the power bank — runs out within days.

Here’s what the official documents actually say. And what prepared British families are already doing about it.

THE DEPENDENCY NOBODY TALKS ABOUT
When the Power Dies, You Go Dark — In Hours

Most people think they’re covered when the lights go out — a torch in a drawer, a charged phone, maybe an old radio somewhere in the loft. But every one of those runs on a battery that dies, with no way to bring it back.

Here’s how fast it falls apart:

HOUR 1 — The lights die. So does the heating. gov.uk is blunt: Gas ovens, boilers, heat pumps and your home internet won’t work without power. The house goes black, then cold.

HOURS 2–6 — The phones fade. Your mobile phone might stop working if your local mast is in the affected area. And today’s digital landlines will not function in a power cut without a backup battery. Calls stop connecting, the internet’s gone, and the news goes with it.

HOURS 6–12 — The batteries run dry. The torch dims, the phone hits zero, and there’s no socket to bring any of it back.

DAY 3 — You’re on your own. The government’s own advice: Being ready for 3 days helps you manage while support reaches those most in need. Those first three days are on you. In a national outage, the Risk Register expects full power back across Great Britain only beyond 7 days.

No light. No news. No way to call out — for your whole street, at the same time.

THE MATHS EVERY FAMILY GETS WRONG
Your Kit Is a Countdown

You think a torch, a charged phone and a drawer of batteries has you covered. Do the maths.

A torch runs a few nights on a set of batteries. A phone gives you a day. A power bank, one more charge. A plug-in radio or smart speaker? Dead the second the power is. Every one of them starts counting down the moment the grid goes down.

Torch = a few nights. Phone = a day. Power bank = one charge. Plug-in radio = nothing.

And this isn’t a doomsday hypothetical. Storm Arwen, November 2021: over one million customers lost power — and nearly 4,000 were off supply for over a week. Storms Austen and Boelo, October 2026: power cuts hit 838,700 homes across Britain in a single weekend. Spain and Portugal, 28 April 2025: a total blackout left tens of millions without trains, traffic lights, cash machines, phone connections and internet — and some areas had no power for 16 hours.

None of those was an attack. That was weather and a failing grid. The government’s National Security Strategy describes something far worse: For the first time in many years, we have to actively prepare for the possibility of the UK homeland coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario.

A drawer of kit only moves one direction: down. And when it hits zero, you’re blind, cut off, and no van is coming up your road.

A drawer of kit isn’t a plan. It’s a deadline.

WHAT PREPARED FAMILIES DO INSTEAD
Stop Stockpiling Kit That Dies. Keep One That Doesn’t.

Here’s what changes everything: the government’s Be Ready checklist, updated on 22 October 2026, tells every UK household to keep three things for a power cut — a torch, an FM radio (battery or wind-up), and a charged power bank.

Yet only 23% of UK adults say they have an FM radio powered by battery, solar or wind-up. And on 31 January 2027, the UK’s copper landline network — the old phone line that kept working in a power cut — is switched off.

Picture your mum. Say she’s 74, on her own in a bungalow outside Inverness, on a January night when the lights go. Her landline is digital now. Her mobile is on 9%. The torch is somewhere in the shed. Does she have any of the three?

Most families who have them keep them scattered across three gadgets in three drawers — and every one runs on a battery that runs out.

So prepared families made one simple change in how they think. They stopped asking how much kit can I stockpile? — because any amount runs out. They started asking what’s the one thing that does it all and never needs a socket? — because that’s what’s still working on day ten.

Daylight comes every morning, even in a British winter. Your own arm never needs recharging. The moment you keep one device that makes its own power, your readiness stops being a pile of batteries in a drawer and becomes something that simply doesn’t quit.

A drawer of kit is a countdown. One device that powers itself never runs out.
